newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens to inaugurate new president amid ruins.
newsitem.headline: Chechens to inaugurate new president amid ruins.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, who led Chechnya's successful resistance to Russia's army, will be sworn in as the rebel region's president on Wednesday amid the ruins left by nearly two years of conflict.

Maskhadov, 45, won an election last month which Chechens said underlined their independence from Russia but which also prompted Moscow to reiterate its refusal to let the small southern region break away.
President Boris Yeltsin, who sent troops to Chechnya in December 1994 to try to stop it splitting away, will send a personal representative to the ceremony.
But few foreign delegations look set to attend. No country has recognised Chechnya's declaration of independence.
The fighting which killed tens of thousands of people ended six months ago and the Russian troops have gone. But the mess they have left behind will take years to clear up.
Maskhadov, a former Soviet artillery colonel who led theguerrilla army against Russian troops and then headed peace talks, faces huge tasks trying to keep order and rebuild his region.
In the regional capital Grozny on Tuesday, the Chemists' House of Culture was getting last-minute repairs as one of the few places still standing where a ceremony could be held.
All the main public buildings in the city centre have been reduced to rubble.

The several hundred armed men designated to look after security for the event are needed because murder, kidnappings and assassination attempts have become common features in a region brutalised by 21 months of fighting.
"We are here to protect the foreign delegations," said interior ministry commander Isa Gadayev.
It was not clear who these foreign delegations would be.

Marbek Bachagayev, spokesman for the inauguration proceedings, said Russia had refused viasas to delegations from Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Turkey and Jordan. The Russian foreign ministry in Moscow was not available for comment.

Other Chechen officials said they were hoping for parliamentary delegations from Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Poland. "Until the last minute we will not know who will come and who will not," one said.
Bachagayev said Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin's former security chief turned rival, had arrived for the ceremony which marks a key step in the peace process he put in place with Maskhadov last August.

Officials delcined to give full details of the ceremony, although it is expected to include a speech by Maskhadov and dancing. He replaces acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev who had stood in for Dzhokhar Dudayev, Chechen president from 1991 until he was killed in a rocket attack last April.
Near the inauguration site, a statue was being beheaded.
"It's some chemist," said one workman disdainfully as another took a hachet to the neck of the likeness of a Russian whose name no one could remember.
In the end they gave up battering the statue gracing the Russia neo-classical Chemists' House of Culture and put a poster of 19th century Chechen hero Imam Shamil in front of it.
A portrait of Dudayev, whose determination to split Chechnya from Russia led to 21 months of conflict, was already hiding the statue on the other side.
In front of the building, freshly-painted pink, a motley group of men with guns, some in military fatigues, others in anoraks and sunglasses, lined up in ragged ranks.
